findings.summary: Criterion 7 is shown with a stand-in requirement, not the acceleration requirement the request names, and its test adds nothing.
findings.evidence: Grep of docs/spec.toml finds no 'acceler', 'measurably' or 'owns its' text. The only statement matching the speed words is spec.toml:928 (learning effectiveness: 'cheaper, faster or more reliable'). BRIEF.md has '### 2026-10-13: Athena owns acceleration' at line 494, before '# Project Olympus' at line 550, so `sections()` in xtask/tests/spec.rs cannot cite it. The planned test `a_requirement_about_speed_records_a_mechanism_or_none_and_an_owner` only repeats what `the_real_spec_passes` already enforces for every active requirement. A mechanism for acceleration does exist (`Athena::throughput_review`, hestia.rs:1040), so the requirement could be given a real mechanism. Fix: Choose one of two routes and state it in the plan. (a) Add one requirement for 'Athena owns acceleration' (and for 'Speed first' if wanted), and allow that heading in `sections()` in xtask/tests/spec.rs, which is a named file. Give it mechanism `Athena::throughput_review` (crates/athena-core/src/hestia.rs), owner hestia and a throughput measure, and have the criterion 7 test look up that id. (b) Ask the user before producing, and record criterion 7 as not met. Do not present learning effectiveness as the acceleration requirement.

findings.summary: Matching speed words in the statement is a crude rule, and its only match today is a false positive.
findings.evidence: Today the keyword list matches exactly one active statement, spec.toml:928. That requirement is about measuring learning effectiveness and mentions 'faster' only in passing. So OP-23 urgency would go to the wrong requirement, while the real speed requirements (acceleration, Speed first) get none. Common words such as 'slower' or 'speed' in future statements would give more false positives. Fix: Take speed from data the plan already adds. For example, a requirement is about speed when its measure names the `throughput` or `check_durations` status section, or when its source heading is a speed or acceleration addendum. Keep this in one function, and test it with a non-speed statement that contains 'faster'.

findings.summary: Treating any measure without a known status section as failing would flag most constraint requirements, and the status line mislabels these gaps.
findings.evidence: The status sections in STATUS_MEASURE_SECTIONS are throughput, check_durations, planning_cost, keep_rule, producer_settings, mistakes, repeated_causes, code_health, audit and audience (status.rs:958-1008). Many of the 135 requirements (constraints, records rules, boundary rules) have no natural place in athena status. They would have to write `status: none` and be flagged as failing, or name a loosely related section just to pass. The per-pass cap of 5 only delays the flood. Step 7 also prints 'requirement <id> has no mechanism' for every gap, including gaps that are only about owner or measure. Fix: Separate 'not shown in status' from 'failing'. A measure fails when it is blank or 'none', or when it names a status section that does not exist. A measure that names a test or check, with no status section, is a valid measure, and status can list it apart from the gaps. Queue requests only for a missing mechanism or a failing measure under that definition. Make the `next` line state the actual reason, and list measure-only gaps under a different label from 'no mechanism'.
findings.location: Plan: Decision 4 (failing measure) and step 7 `next` line

findings.summary: If the user closes a spec-gap request as unwanted, the next drain queues it again.
findings.evidence: In Decision 3, only open requests stop a new one being queued, so a request closed by the user is queued again at the next drain start. The only ways to stop this are to edit the spec or mark the requirement superseded, and the plan does not say so. Fix: State this as intended in the request body (the way to stop it is to fill the mechanism or supersede the requirement). Or treat a request closed by a person as addressing the gap until the spec text for that id changes.

findings.summary: The section names are Rust field names in StatusView, not the headings a reader sees in athena status.
findings.evidence: The drift test checks for `pub <name>:` fields in status.rs, but the request asks the measure to say 'where in athena status', which a reader finds by the printed headings. Fix: Use the labels that athena status prints (or show the mapping from field to label), so the measure points to something a reader can find.

summary: I read the plan's claims against the snapshot and they hold up. docs/spec.toml has 135 `status = "active"` lines. toml_edit is already a dependency of athena-core (Cargo.toml line 26). `Athena::review_passes` (hestia.rs:1410) runs at every sweep and drain start. `default_checks` and `the_skeleton_registers_no_checks` exist, as do `Athena::queue` (reading.rs:735), `Athena::close` (manage.rs:74) and `Athena::status` (status.rs:1483). The Requirement struct in xtask/tests/spec.rs uses deny_unknown_fields. Running the check as a review pass, deduping by a whole-line id marker, and adding no dependency are all sound choices. Two problems remain. First, criterion 7 is met only by a stand-in. The requirement the request names, that Athena gets faster and owns its acceleration, is not in the spec at all. The only active statement that matches the plan's speed words is OLY learning-effectiveness (spec.toml:928), and the criterion 7 test adds nothing beyond the general rule. Second, two of the plan's rules match on wording and will wrongly flag many requirements. Speed is guessed from words in the statement, and its only match today is that learning-effectiveness requirement, which is not about Athena's speed. A measure counts as failing when it names no athena status section. Most constraint-type requirements have no such section, so the sweep would gradually queue a request for most of the spec, and the producer is pushed to name a loosely related section just to avoid the flag. These can be fixed in the plan, so the verdict is revise.
